claim: Metastasis suppressor 1 (Mtss1) ensured axonal extension while sensitizing axons to the Semaphorin 3E (Sema3E)-Plexin-D1 repulsive cue.
source: metastasis suppressor 1 (Mtss1), a membrane protrusion protein, ensured axonal extension while sensitizing axons to the Semaphorin 3E (Sema3E)-Plexin-D1 repulsive cue.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, including neurite outgrowth assays and growth cone collapse assays.

claim: Sema3E-Plexin-D1 signaling enhanced Mtss1 expression in projecting striatonigral neurons.
source: Sema3E-Plexin-D1 signaling enhanced Mtss1 expression in projecting striatonigral neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data, qRT-PCR, western blot analysis, and in situ hybridization experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Mtss1 localized to the neurite axonal side and regulated neurite outgrowth in cultured neurons.
source: Mtss1 localized to the neurite axonal side and regulated neurite outgrowth in cultured neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data showing Mtss1 localization to Tau-positive axonal regions and neurite length measurements in cultured neurons.

claim: Mtss1 aided Plexin-D1 trafficking to the growth cone, where it signaled a repulsive cue to Sema3E.
source: Mtss1 also aided Plexin-D1 trafficking to the growth cone, where it signaled a repulsive cue to Sema3E.
evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging of Plexin-D1-GFP vesicles, AP-Sema3E binding assays, and colocalization studies in growth cones.

claim: Mtss1 ablation reduced neurite extension and growth cone collapse in cultured neurons.
source: Mtss1 ablation reduced neurite extension and growth cone collapse in cultured neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by neurite length measurements and growth cone collapse assays in Mtss1-knockout neurons shown in Figures 3 and 6.

claim: Mtss1-knockout mice exhibited fewer striatonigral projections and irregular axonal routes.
source: Mtss1-knockout mice exhibited fewer striatonigral projections and irregular axonal routes
evidence: This claim is supported by AP-Sema3E binding assays, immunohistochemistry, and DiI tracing experiments in Mtss1-knockout mice shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: The striatonigral projection defects in Mtss1-knockout mice were recapitulated in Plxnd1- or Sema3e-knockout mice.
source: these defects were recapitulated in Plxnd1- or Sema3e-knockout mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis of striatonigral projections in Mtss1-, Plxnd1-, and Sema3e-knockout mice shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Repulsive axon guidance activates an exquisite autoregulatory program coordinating both axonal extension and steering during neuronal pathfinding.
source: These findings demonstrate that repulsive axon guidance activates an exquisite autoregulatory program coordinating both axonal extension and steering during neuronal pathfinding.
evidence: This claim is based on the integration of multiple experimental findings showing that Sema3E-Plexin-D1 signaling induces Mtss1 expression, which in turn regulates both axonal growth and guidance.

claim: Bulk RNA sequencing identified 2360 differentially expressed transcripts in Plxnd1-knockout mice compared to wild-type mice at P5.
source: Application of a conservative DEseq approach to RNA-seq data analysis confirmed 2360 differentially expressed transcripts (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by RNA-seq data analysis presented in Figure 1 and supplementary figures.

claim: Mtss1 gene expression was downregulated in Plxnd1-knockout striatal tissues at P5.
source: Mtss1 gene expression was verified by quantitative RT-PCR (qRT-PCR) performed with Plxnd1-knockout striatal tissues (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Mtss1 protein levels were markedly decreased in Plxnd1-knockout mice at P5.
source: The Mtss1 protein levels were also markedly decreased in the knockout mice at P5 (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: Mtss1 expression was decreased in Sema3e-knockout striatal samples at P5, but less dramatically than in Plxnd1-knockout samples.
source: We also analyzed Mtss1 expression in Sema3e-knockout striatal samples obtained at P5 and found that its expression was decreased, but less dramatically than it was in Plxnd1-knockout striatal samples (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis comparing Mtss1 expression in Sema3e-knockout and Plxnd1-knockout mice shown in Figure 1F and G.

claim: Sema3E-Plexin-D1 signaling activation can increase Mtss1 expression in striatal neurons during development.
source: These results suggest that Sema3E-Plexin-D1 signaling activation can increase Mtss1 expression in striatal neurons during development.
evidence: This claim is based on the observation that Mtss1 expression is reduced in both Plxnd1- and Sema3e-knockout mice.

claim: Mtss1 expression significantly overlapped with Plxnd1-positive neurons in both the cortex and striatum.
source: Mtss1 expression significantly overlapped with Plxnd1-positive neurons in both the cortex and striatum, and its expression was reduced in Plxnd1-knockout mice (Figure 1H and I).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1H and I.

claim: 98.2 ± 1.72% of Mtss1 expression overlapped with Drd1a-tdT striatal neurons.
source: Mtss1 expression significantly overlapped with Drd1a-tdT striatal neurons (Figure 1J; 98.2 ± 1.72%)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data in Drd1a-tdT mice shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Mtss1 is selectively expressed in striatonigral projecting MSNs under Plexin-D1 signaling.
source: suggesting that Plexin-D1 signaling mediates Mtss1 expression selectively in striatonigral projecting MSNs.
evidence: This claim is based on the high overlap between Mtss1 and Drd1a-tdT expression, and the reduction of Mtss1 in Plxnd1-knockout mice.

claim: Mtss1 was expressed at a low level regardless of Plexin-D1 presence at E16.5.
source: Although Mtss1 was expressed at a low level regardless of Plexin-D1 presence at E16.5, it seemed to be under the control of Plexin-D1 signaling in the developing striatum from the last gestation period to the early postnatal period (Figure 1K and L).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis at different developmental stages shown in Figure 1K and L.

claim: Sema3E ligand was predominantly expressed in the thalamus and released into the striatum during thalamostriatal projection at E16.5.
source: Furthermore, the Sema3E ligand activating the Plexin-D1 receptor was predominantly expressed in the thalamus and released into the striatum, probably during thalamostriatal projection at E16.5, as observed in the early postnatal stage in a previous study (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Ding et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization and AP-Plexin-D1-ECD binding data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2, and cited from a previous study.

claim: Both Plexin-D1 and Mtss1 were expressed in the embryonic striatum, and their expression was elevated in the perinatal stage.
source: Both Plexin-D1 and Mtss1 were expressed in the embryonic striatum, and their expression was elevated in the perinatal stage.
evidence: This claim is supported by temporal expression analysis shown in Figure 1M and N.

claim: Mtss1 expression was maintained at a relatively high level from E18.5 to P5 and then declined sharply and disappeared in the adult striatum.
source: Interestingly, Mtss1 expression was maintained at a relatively high level from E18.5 to P5 and then declined sharply and disappeared in the adult striatum
evidence: This claim is supported by temporal expression analysis shown in Figure 1M and N.

claim: Plexin-D1 expression was maintained at a low level in the adult striatum.
source: although Plexin-D1 showed a similar expression pattern, its expression was maintained at a low level in the adult striatum, presumably to regulate other functions such as thalamostriatal synapse formation (Figure 1M and N; Ding et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by temporal expression analysis shown in Figure 1M and N, and cited from a previous study.

claim: In wild-type neurons, both Plexin-D1 and Mtss1 expression levels were low at DIV3 and then increased by DIV6.
source: In wild-type neurons, both Plexin-D1 and Mtss1 expression levels were low at day 3 in vitro (DIV3) and then increased by DIV6.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis of cultured neurons shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Plxnd1-knockout neurons failed to elevate Mtss1 expression by DIV6.
source: In contrast, Plxnd1-knockout neurons failed to elevate Mtss1 expression by DIV6, suggesting that Mtss1 expression is induced at the cellular level rather than by indirect systemic changes at the circuit level in vivo (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis of cultured Plxnd1-knockout neurons shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Mtss1 expression was decreased in cultured Sema3e-knockout neurons.
source: In addition, the expression of Mtss1 was decreased in cultured Sema3e-knockout neurons (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis of cultured Sema3e-knockout neurons shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Mtss1 expression was increased by Sema3E replenishment in Sema3e-knockout neurons.
source: In fact, Mtss1 expression was increased by Sema3E replenishment in Sema3e-knockout neurons, whereas it was not altered in Plxnd1-knockout neurons (Figure 2F–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis after AP-Sema3E treatment shown in Figure 2F-I.

claim: Treatment with Akt inhibitor MK2206 downregulated Mtss1 expression but caused no changes in Plexin-D1 levels.
source: Treatment with an Akt inhibitor, MK2206, downregulated Mtss1 expression but caused no changes in Plexin-D1 levels (Figure 2J–M).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis after MK2206 treatment shown in Figure 2J-M.

claim: The elevated expression of Mtss1 due to exogenous Sema3E supplement in Sema3e-knockout neurons was diminished by MK2206.
source: Furthermore, the elevated expression of Mtss1 due to the addition of exogenous Sema3E supplement in Sema3e-knockout neurons was also diminished by MK2206, suggesting that the Sema3E-Plexin-D1 pathway is involved in Mtss1 expression through Akt signaling (Figure 2N and O).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis after combined AP-Sema3E and MK2206 treatment shown in Figure 2N and O.

claim: Mtss1 is a downstream expression target of Sema3E-Plexin-D1 signaling in direct-pathway MSNs.
source: These results suggest that Mtss1 is a downstream expression target of Sema3E-Plexin-D1 signaling in direct-pathway MSNs.
evidence: This claim is based on multiple experiments showing that Mtss1 expression is regulated by Sema3E-Plexin-D1 signaling through Akt.

claim: Mtss1 overexpression in COS7 cells led to diverse morphological changes such as excessively spiky or thin and long processes.
source: Mtss1 overexpression in COS7 cells led to a diverse degree of morphological changes, such as excessively spiky or thin and long processes, and highly localized in F-actin-enriched protrusions.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data in COS7 cells shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Overexpression of Mtss1 lacking the I-BAR domain failed to generate protrusive shapes in COS7 cells.
source: However, overexpression of Mtss1 lacking the I-BAR domain failed to generate these protrusive shapes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data in COS7 cells shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Mtss1 was significantly localized to the Tau-positive-axonal side of cultured MSNs at DIV3.
source: Interestingly, Mtss1 was significantly localized to the Tau-positive-axonal side of cultured MSNs at DIV3 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data showing colocalization of Mtss1 with Tau in Figure 3A.

claim: Significant growth retardation was observed in MSNs lacking Mtss1 compared to wild-type neurons at DIV3 and DIV6.
source: We observed significant growth retardation in MSNs lacking Mtss1 compared to wild-type neurons at DIV3 and DIV6 (Figure 3B, C and E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by neurite length measurements in Mtss1-knockout neurons shown in Figure 3B, C, E, and F.

claim: Mtss1-deficient neurons failed to extend neurites more than twice the size of the cell body.
source: Furthermore, we also observed that Mtss1-deficient neurons failed to extend neurites more than twice the size of the cell body, suggesting that a lack of Mtss1 presumably caused a severe neurite growth defect (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of neurons with short neurites shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There was no difference in neurite length between Drd1a-positive wild-type MSNs and Plxnd1-knockout MSNs at DIV3.
source: Interestingly, there was no difference in neurite length between Drd1a-positive wild-type MSNs and Plxnd1-knockout MSNs at DIV3 (Figure 3G and H), probably due to the low Mtss1 induction shown in Figure 2A
evidence: This claim is supported by neurite length measurements in Plxnd1-knockout neurons at DIV3 shown in Figure 3G and H.

claim: Neurite length was significantly reduced in Plxnd1-deficient MSNs at DIV6.
source: whereas the length was significantly reduced in the Plxnd1-deficient MSNs at DIV6 (Figure 3I and J).
evidence: This claim is supported by neurite length measurements in Plxnd1-knockout neurons at DIV6 shown in Figure 3I and J.

claim: Ectopic Mtss1 overexpression rescued the growth reduction phenotype in Plxnd1-knockout neurons.
source: In comparison to the neurite length observed in GFP-overexpressing MSNs, ectopic Mtss1 overexpression rescued the growth reduction phenotype in the Plxnd1-knockout neurons (Figure 3K and L).
evidence: This claim is supported by neurite length measurements after Mtss1 overexpression in Plxnd1-knockout neurons shown in Figure 3K and L.

claim: The Sema3E-Plexin-D1 repulsive guidance cue is capable of regulating axonal growth through positive facilitator proteins such as Mtss1.
source: These results suggest that the Sema3E-Plexin-D1 repulsive guidance cue is capable of regulating axonal growth through positive facilitator proteins such as Mtss1.
evidence: This claim is based on the rescue of neurite growth defects by Mtss1 overexpression in Plxnd1-knockout neurons.

claim: Full-length Plexin-D1 and Mtss1 were successfully pulled down together when overexpressed in HEK293T cells.
source: When we overexpressed full-length Plexin-D1 and Mtss1 together in HEK293T cells, both proteins were successfully pulled down together (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Plexin-D1 with the intracellular domain (ICD) deleted failed to bind Mtss1.
source: However, Plexin-D1 with the intracellular domain (ICD) deleted failed to bind Mtss1, indicating an intracellular Plexin-D1 and Mtss1 interaction (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by coimmunoprecipitation data with Plexin-D1ΔICD shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Every Mtss1 construct containing the I-BAR domain coprecipitated with Plexin-D1, but I-BAR-deficient Mtss1 failed to interact with Plexin-D1.
source: When we overexpressed full-length Plexin-D1 and each Mtss1 deletion construct, every Mtss1 construct containing the I-BAR domain coprecipitated with Plexin-D1, but I-BAR-deficient Mtss1 failed to interact with Plexin-D1 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by coimmunoprecipitation data with Mtss1 deletion constructs shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Plexin-D1 forms a complex with SH3BP1.
source: As previously reported, we found that overexpression of Plexin-D1 in HEK293T cells resulted in the formation of a complex with overexpressed SH3BP1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and cited from previous studies.

claim: Plexin-D1 did not form a complex with srGAP2 or IRSP53.
source: However, it did not form a complex with srGAP2, a protein containing an F-BAR domain, or IRSP53, another protein containing an I-BAR domain like Mtss1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Mtss1 was unable to form a complex with Plexin-B2 or Plexin-B3 proteins.
source: As shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and E, overexpressed Mtss1 was unable to form a complex with Plexin-B2 or -B3 proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: The formation of the Plexin-D1-Mtss1 complex is relatively specific.
source: These findings suggest that the formation of the Plexin-D1-Mtss1 complex is relatively specific.
evidence: This claim is based on the observation that Plexin-D1 does not bind to other BAR domain proteins and Mtss1 does not bind to other Plexin family members.

claim: Sema3E treatment did not interfere with Plexin-D1-Mtss1 complex formation.
source: In contrast to the effect on SH3BP1, Sema3E treatment did not interfere with Plexin-D1-Mtss1 complex formation, indicating that the complex is formed in a Sema3E-independent manner (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by coimmunoprecipitation data after Sema3E treatment shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: Plexin-D1 and Mtss1 can bind directly to each other.
source: As shown in Figure 4G, both proteins precipitated together, suggesting that Plexin-D1 and Mtss1 play a role as direct binding partners.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro protein-protein binding assay using purified proteins shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Mtss1 coexpression did not change the Plexin-D1 protein level on the cell surface in COS7 cells.
source: We observed that overexpressed Plexin-D1 proteins in COS7 cells were efficiently biotinylated on the cell surface, but the Plexin-D1 protein level on the surface was not changed during Mtss1 coexpression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by surface biotinylation assay shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Mtss1 coexpression did not affect Sema3E-induced Plexin-D1 endocytosis.
source: However, Mtss1 coexpression did not affect Sema3E-induced Plexin-D1 endocytosis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by endocytosis assay shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Mtss1 overexpression did not change the binding affinity of Sema3E for Plexin-D1.
source: Additionally, Mtss1 overexpression did not change the binding affinity of Sema3E for Plexin-D1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by AP-Sema3E binding assay shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: When Plexin-D1 and Mtss1 were coexpressed in COS7 cells, both proteins were mostly present in F-actin-enriched protrusions.
source: As shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and G, when Plexin-D1 and Mtss1 were coexpressed, both proteins were mostly present in F-actin-enriched protrusions.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data in COS7 cells shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and G.

claim: Overexpression of Plexin-D1 lacking the ICD overlapped with Mtss1 to a lesser extent than overexpression of wild-type Plexin-D1.
source: However, overexpression of Plexin-D1 lacking the ICD overlapped with Mtss1 to a lesser extent than overexpression of wild-type Plexin-D1, whereas Mtss1 was abundant in the protrusions.
evidence: This claim is supported by colocalization analysis in COS7 cells shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and G.

claim: Mtss1 lacking the I-BAR domain did not generate filopodia-like protrusions in COS7 cells but was localized with F-actin.
source: In addition, Mtss1 lacking the I-BAR domain, which possesses membrane-bending activity, did not generate filopodia-like protrusions in COS7 cells but was localized with F-actin, including in marginal areas, probably via the Mtss1 WH2 domain (Mattila et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data in COS7 cells shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and G, and cited from a previous study.

claim: The localization of Plexin-D1 and Mtss1 in the protrusions was not disturbed in the presence of Sema3E.
source: In addition, the localization of Plexin-D1 and Mtss1 in the protrusions was also not disturbed in the presence of Sema3E (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data after Sema3E treatment shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Both overexpressed Plexin-D1 and Mtss1 proteins seemed to be colocalized along growing neurites in Mtss1-deficient striatal neurons.
source: Both overexpressed Plexin-D1 and Mtss1 proteins seemed to be colocalized along growing neurites, but the Mtss1 mutant lacking the I-BAR domain showed reduced Plexin-D1 level as well as a low colocalization rate (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry and colocalization analysis in neurons shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Wild-type Mtss1 proteins were present with Plexin-D1 in F-actin-enriched regions of growth cones.
source: As shown in COS7 cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F), wild-type Mtss1 proteins were present with Plexin-D1 in F-actin-enriched regions of growth cones
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data in growth cones shown in Figure 5D-F.

claim: Mutant Mtss1 lacking the I-BAR domain was expressed at a lower level than wild-type Mtss1 and failed to colocalize with Plexin-D1, resulting in reduced Plexin-D1 localization in the growth cone.
source: in contrast, mutant Mtss1 was expressed at a lower level than wild-type Mtss1 and failed to colocalize with Plexin-D1, resulting in reduced Plexin-D1 localization in the growth cone (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry and quantification in growth cones shown in Figure 5D-F.

claim: The majority of Plexin-D1-containing vesicles were dynamically transported in both proximal and distal directions in wild-type MSNs.
source: Our live-cell imaging showed that the majority of Plexin-D1-containing vesicles were dynamically transported in both proximal and distal directions in wild-type MSNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 5G-K and Videos 1-4.

claim: Plexin-D1-positive vesicles in Mtss1-deficient MSNs remained stationary, and their overall numbers in neurites were slightly reduced.
source: In contrast, the Plexin-D1-positive vesicles in Mtss1-deficient MSNs remained stationary, and their overall numbers in neurites were also slightly reduced (Figure 5G–K and Videos 1–4).
evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data and quantification shown in Figure 5G-K and Videos 1-4.

claim: Mtss1 contributes to the dynamic transportation of Plexin-D1 along the growing neurites of direct-pathway MSNs.
source: These observations demonstrate that Mtss1 facilitates the dynamic transportation of Plexin-D1 along the growing neurites of direct-pathway MSNs, leading to an increased rate of Plexin-D1 localization in the growth cones.
evidence: This claim is based on the observation that Plexin-D1 vesicle movement is reduced in Mtss1-deficient neurons.

claim: Mtss1-knockout neurons exhibited a low level of AP-Sema3E binding in the growth cones.
source: The Mtss1-knockout neurons exhibited a low level of AP-Sema3E binding in the growth cones, indicating that the endogenous trafficking of Plexin-D1 to the tip of the growing axon is disrupted in the absence of Mtss1 (Figure 5L and M).
evidence: This claim is supported by AP-Sema3E binding assay in growth cones shown in Figure 5L and M.

claim: Mtss1 serves to deliver Plexin-D1 to the growth cone.
source: These results suggest that Mtss1 serves to deliver Plexin-D1 to the growth cone.
evidence: This claim is based on multiple experiments showing reduced Plexin-D1 localization and trafficking in the absence of Mtss1.

claim: Wild-type Drd1a-tdT-positive striatal neurons underwent a high collapse rate after exogenous Sema3E treatment.
source: we performed a growth cone collapse assay at DIV3 in direct-pathway MSNs and found that wild-type Drd1a-tdT-positive striatal neurons underwent a high collapse rate after exogenous Sema3E treatment
evidence: This claim is supported by growth cone collapse assay data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: The growth cones of neurons lacking Mtss1 did not collapse at a significantly different rate after Sema3E treatment.
source: whereas the growth cones of neurons lacking Mtss1 did not collapse at a significantly different rate (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth cone collapse assay data in Mtss1-knockout neurons shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Reintroduction of wild-type Mtss1 into Mtss1-knockout MSNs resulted in growth cone collapse.
source: However, reintroduction of wild-type Mtss1 into Mtss1-knockout MSNs resulted in growth cone collapse, but overexpressed Mtss1 lacking the I-BAR domain showed less response to Sema3E (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth cone collapse assay after Mtss1 rescue shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: Plxnd1-null MSNs showed a very low collapse rate regardless of Sema3E addition at DIV6.
source: In addition, Plxnd1-null MSNs also showed a very low collapse rate regardless of Sema3E addition at DIV6 (Figure 6E), consistent with a previous report that Sema3E-Plexin-D1 signaling acts as a repulsive guidance cue (Chauvet et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth cone collapse assay in Plxnd1-knockout neurons shown in Figure 6E, and cited from a previous study.

claim: The reduced collapse phenotypes in Plxnd1-knockout neurons were rescued by overexpression of full-length Plexin-D1 but not by ICD-deleted Plexin-D1.
source: The reduced collapse phenotypes were rescued by overexpression of full-length Plexin-D1 but not by ICD-deleted Plexin-D1 (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth cone collapse assay after Plexin-D1 rescue shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Mtss1 targeting of Plexin-D1 to the growth cone is critical for robust Sema3E-induced repulsive signaling.
source: In summary, Mtss1 targeting of Plexin-D1 to the growth cone is critical for robust Sema3E-induced repulsive signaling.
evidence: This claim is based on the observation that growth cone collapse in response to Sema3E is impaired in Mtss1-knockout neurons.

claim: Mtss1 was localized in the striatonigral tract and SNr in wild-type mice.
source: We observed Mtss1 localization in the striatonigral tract and SNr, but the immunostaining signal disappeared in Mtss1-deficient mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mtss1-knockout mice exhibited a relatively small area of Plexin-D1-positive striatonigral tracts at E17.5.
source: In contrast, Mtss1-knockout mice exhibited a relatively small area of Plexin-D1-positive striatonigral tracts, including both poor neuronal projection and reduced Plexin-D1 localization at E17.5 (Figure 7A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by AP-Sema3E binding assay and neurofilament staining shown in Figure 7A-D.

claim: The density of the AP-Sema3E-positive tracts was reduced in Mtss1-knockout mice at E17.5.
source: In addition, despite these reduced neuronal projections in the Mtss1-knockout mice, the density of the AP-Sema3E-positive tracts was reduced even more (Figure 7E), indicating that the absence of Mtss1 prevents both normal axonal projections and Plexin-D1 trafficking.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of AP and neurofilament density shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The bundle density of Plexin-D1-positive projections passing between the rTh and Gp was reduced in Mtss1-knockout mice at E17.5.
source: In the coronal view, the bundle density of Plexin-D1-positive projections passing between the rTh and Gp was reduced in the Mtss1-knockout mice (Figure 7F).
evidence: This claim is supported by AP-Sema3E binding assay in coronal sections shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Mtss1-deficient neonates showed fewer Plexin-D1-positive striatonigral projections in the coverage area and a reduced path width at P5.
source: Consistent with the results obtained with E17.5 embryos, Mtss1-deficient neonates showed fewer Plexin-D1-positive striatonigral projections in the coverage area and a reduced path width (Figure 7G–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by AP-Sema3E binding assay at P5 shown in Figure 7G-J.

claim: The total boundary area with Drd1a-tdT-positive projections was smaller and less compact in Mtss1-knockout mice than in wild-type mice at P5.
source: Consistent with the results shown in AP-Sema3E binding experiments, the total boundary area with Drd1a-tdT-positive projections was smaller and less compact in the Mtss1-knockout mice than in the wild-type mice at P5 (Figure 7K–M).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry of Drd1a-tdT projections shown in Figure 7K-M.

claim: At P30, the projection density defects were more obvious in Mtss1-knockout mice, but the boundary area was not significantly different from wild-type mice.
source: At P30, the projection density defects were more obvious, but the boundary area in the wild-type and mutant mice was not significantly different, indicating that Mtss1 deficiency led to the formation of fewer striatonigral axonal bundles (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry of Drd1a-tdT projections at P30 shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: A decreased ratio of AP-Sema3E binding per tdT staining was observed in Mtss1-knockout mice at P5.
source: Our findings revealed a decreased ratio of AP-Sema3E binding per tdT staining, suggesting that Mtss1 is implicated not only in axonal projections but also in Plexin-D1 trafficking in navigating striatonigral projections (Figure 7N–Q).
evidence: This claim is supported by combined AP-Sema3E binding and tdT staining analysis shown in Figure 7N-Q.

claim: Few dying cells were found in wild-type and Mtss1-mutant neonates using cleaved caspase 3 staining.
source: Using cleaved caspase 3 staining to detect apoptotic cells, we found few dying cells in the wild-type and Mtss1-mutant neonates (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A and B), indicating that no significant cell pathology was induced by Mtss1 expression deficiency.
evidence: This claim is supported by cleaved caspase 3 immunostaining shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: No detectable difference in dendritic morphology was found between wild-type and Mtss1 mutants at P5 using Golgi staining.
source: However, we found no detectable difference between the wild-type and Mtss1 mutants at P5 (Figure 7—figure supplement 3C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Golgi staining and Sholl analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3C-E.

claim: No significant change in Plexin-D1 levels was observed in the striatum or cultured neurons of Mtss1-deficient mice compared to littermate controls.
source: In addition, no significant change in Plexin-D1 levels was observed in the striatum or cultured neurons of Mtss1-deficient mice compared to those in littermate controls (Figure 7—figure supplement 3F–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3F-I.

claim: The weakening of the Plexin-D1-positive striatonigral pathway in Mtss1-knockout mice is caused by both impairments of neuronal projections and inappropriate Plexin-D1 distribution.
source: These results indicate that the weakening of the Plexin-D1-positive striatonigral pathway in Mtss1-knockout mice is caused by both impairments of neuronal projections and inappropriate Plexin-D1 distribution due to Mtss1 downregulation.
evidence: This claim is based on the combined observations of reduced projections and reduced Plexin-D1 localization in Mtss1-knockout mice.

claim: The boundary area and compactness of descending striatonigral projections were small and loose in Plxnd1-knockout mice during the neonatal period.
source: During the neonatal period, the boundary area and compactness of descending striatonigral projections were small and loose in the Plxnd1-knockout mice, but only a reduced projection density was observed in adult mice, which was similar to that of Mtss1-knockout mice (Figure 7R–T, Figure 7—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry of Drd1a-tdT projections in Plxnd1-knockout mice shown in Figure 7R-T and Figure 7—figure supplement 2D-F.

claim: Sema3e-knockout at P5 showed striatonigral projection defects, albeit somewhat milder compared to Plxnd1- or Mtss1-deficient mice.
source: Moreover, Sema3e-knockout at P5 also showed these projection defects, albeit somewhat milder compared to those observed in Plxnd1- or Mtss1-deficient mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 4A–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry of Drd1a-tdT projections in Sema3e-knockout mice shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4A-E.

claim: Activation of Sema3E-Plexin-D1 signaling, which leads to induction of Mtss1, is required for the striatonigral trajectory during the axonal pathfinding period.
source: These phenocopy results suggest that activation of Sema3E-Plexin-D1 signaling, which leads to induction of Mtss1, is required for the striatonigral trajectory during the axonal pathfinding period.
evidence: This claim is based on the similar phenotypes observed in Mtss1-, Plxnd1-, and Sema3e-knockout mice.

claim: The descending striatonigral projections in wild-type mice were relatively straight and untangled near the Gp region.
source: Interestingly, we observed that the descending striatonigral projections in the wild-type mice were relatively straight and untangled near the Gp region through the sagittal view (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry of Drd1a-tdT projections shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The axonal bundles appeared relatively fasciculated and straight in wild-type mice at P5 when visualized using 3D imaging by sparsely labeling with DiI injection.
source: When visualizing the striatonigral projection using 3D imaging by sparsely labeling with DiI injection at the dorsal striatum, the axonal bundles appeared relatively fasciculated and straight in the wild-type at P5 (Figure 8B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by 3D imaging of DiI-labeled projections shown in Figure 8B and C.

claim: Mtss1 mutants showed irregular projection patterns with random directionality and mild defasciculation.
source: However, Mtss1 mutants showed irregular projection patterns with random directionality and mild defasciculation (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and 3D imaging in Mtss1-knockout mice shown in Figure 8A-C.

claim: The deficiency of Mtss1 led to more deviant ectopic projections.
source: The deficiency of Mtss1 led to more deviant ectopic projections (Figure 8E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of intersecting axonal bundles shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The misguidance defects were not apparent at P30 in Mtss1-knockout mice.
source: However, the misguidance defects were not apparent at P30, likely because abnormal projections were discarded as mice matured into adults (Figure 7—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry at P30 shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2G.

claim: Inefficient Plexin-D1 trafficking to the extending axons in Mtss1-knockout mice may have weakened the proper guidance response.
source: These results suggest that inefficient Plexin-D1 trafficking to the extending axons in the Mtss1-knockout mice may have weakened the proper guidance response.
evidence: This claim is based on the observation of irregular projection patterns in Mtss1-knockout mice.

claim: Irregular projection patterns were observed near the Gp in Plxnd1-knockout mice at P5 but not at P30.
source: we also observed irregular projection patterns near the Gp in Plxnd1-knockout mice at P5 but not at P30 (Figure 8D and F, Figure 7—figure supplement 2H), similar to those seen in Mtss1-knockout mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry in Plxnd1-knockout mice shown in Figure 8D and F, and Figure 7—figure supplement 2H.

claim: Sema3e-knockout at P5 showed a few axonal bundles deviated from their typical trajectories.
source: Moreover, Sema3e-knockout at P5 showed a few axonal bundles deviated from their typical trajectories (Figure 7—figure supplement 4F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry in Sema3e-knockout mice shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4F and G.

claim: Sema3E-Plexin-D1 signaling, probably in concert with Mtss1 molecules, is specifically involved in the proper guidance of descending striatonigral projections.
source: These results demonstrate that Sema3E-Plexin-D1 signaling, probably in concert with Mtss1 molecules, is specifically involved in the proper guidance of descending striatonigral projections.
evidence: This claim is based on the similar irregular projection patterns observed in Mtss1-, Plxnd1-, and Sema3e-knockout mice.

claim: Mtss1 was not detected in vascular endothelial cells expressing Plexin-D1 during development.
source: Although it was expressed in neuronal cells, Mtss1 was not detected in vascular endothelial cells expressing Plexin-D1 during development (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mtss1-knockout mice did not result in an obvious intersomatic vasculature defect.
source: In addition, Mtss1-knockout mice did not result in an obvious intersomatic vasculature defect, which is a typical phenotype observed in Sema3e or Plxnd1 mutants (Burk et al., 2017; Gu et al., 2005; Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by 3D vascular reconstruction analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B, and cited from previous studies.

claim: Mtss1 was highly expressed in two different types of cultured endothelial cells but was not controlled by Sema3E-Plexin-D1 signaling.
source: Interestingly, Mtss1 was highly expressed in the two different types of cultured endothelial cells but was not controlled by Sema3E-Plexin-D1 signaling (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis in HUVECs and HCMEC/D3 cells shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The activation of Mtss1 by the Sema3E-Plexin-D1 signaling pathway and its function in neurons could be selective and distinct.
source: These results provide evidence that the activation of Mtss1 by the Sema3E-Plexin-D1 signaling pathway and its function in neurons could be selective and distinct.
evidence: This claim is based on the observation that Mtss1 is not regulated by Sema3E-Plexin-D1 in endothelial cells but is in neurons.

claim: Axon guidance molecules regulate directionality and growth pace during nervous system development.
source: Axon guidance molecules are critical for neuronal pathfinding because they regulate directionality and growth pace during nervous system development.
evidence: This is a general statement about axon guidance molecules supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: The molecular mechanisms coordinating proper axonal extension and turning are poorly understood.
source: However, the molecular mechanisms coordinating proper axonal extension and turning are poorly understood.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Plexin-D1 is expressed only in direct-pathway medium spiny neurons (MSNs) projecting to the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr).
source: Notably, Plexin-D1 is expressed only in direct-pathway medium spiny neurons (MSNs) projecting to the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr), one of two distinct types of MSNs in the striatum (Ding et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is cited from a previous study.

claim: Plexin-D1-positive striatonigral axons travel through the corridor between the globus pallidus (Gp) and reticular thalamic nucleus (rTh)/zona incerta (ZI), where Sema3E molecules reside.
source: Plexin-D1-positive striatonigral axons travel through the corridor between the globus pallidus (Gp) and reticular thalamic nucleus (rTh)/zona incerta (ZI), in which Sema3E molecules reside and emit repulsive signals to direct proper pathway formation toward the SNr (Chauvet et al., 2007; Ehrman et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is cited from previous studies.

claim: Approximately 45% of striatal neurons are Plexin-D1-positive neurons.
source: In a previous study, we found that Plxnd1 is selectively expressed in direct-pathway MSNs (also called striatonigral neurons) that project directly to the substantia nigra, with approximately 45% of striatal neurons identified as Plexin-D1-positive neurons (Ding et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is cited from a previous study.

claim: Akt is known to mediate the Sema3E-Plexin-D1 signaling cascade in neurons.
source: Moreover, since Akt is already known to mediate the Sema3E-Plexin-D1 signaling cascade in neurons (Burk et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is cited from a previous study.

claim: Mtss1 has a well-characterized role in the regulation of filopodia and spine precursors.
source: Since Mtss1 has a well-characterized role in the regulation of filopodia and spine precursors (Saarikangas et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is cited from previous studies.

claim: The WH2 domain is an important region for Mtss1 interaction with F-actin.
source: Mtss1 lacking WH2 domain showed much weaker effect because WH2 is an important region for Mtss1 interaction with F-actin (Mattila et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is cited from a previous study.

claim: The pathway establishment of striatonigral projections ends by P7.
source: We assumed that Mtss1 regulates the initial striatonigral axonal projection during development of the neonate and that the pathway establishment ends by P7 (Morello et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is cited from a previous study.

claim: Global Mtss1-mutant mice have enlarged brain ventricles and decreased cortical thickness.
source: Since global Mtss1-mutant mice have enlarged brain ventricles and decreased cortical thickness (Minkeviciene et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is cited from a previous study.
